items.title: The GATE Framework: A Generative AI-Enhanced Active Learning Environment for Tourism Communication Competency Development
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being adopted in tourism and hospitality education more quickly than the pedagogical guidance needed to use it well. This study developed the GATE Framework, a GenAI-enhanced active learning environment intended to develop tourism communication competency, and examined its appropriateness through expert review. The work comprised two stages within the first research phase. An evidence-informed synthesis established three connected layers: Inputs, Core Process Components, and Outcomes. At the center of the Process Layer is an iterative Explore-Generate-Apply-Reflect cycle, supported by human-AI interaction, authentic tourism tasks, peer and instructor participation, reflection, and adaptive feedback. In the second stage, nine experts in tourism and hospitality, curriculum and instruction, educational technology, AI in education, and active learning then evaluated the framework using an 18-item, five-point scale and four open-ended questions. The overall rating was very high (x̄ = 4.54, S.D. = 0.58), and the five domain means ranged from 4.52 to 4.56. The experts gave their strongest ratings to the framework's theoretical alignment, relevance to tourism communication learning, and suitability for further development. Ratings remained favorable but were lower for the definition of individual roles and the practical sequence of the learning process. In response, the framework was revised to clarify scaffolding and human oversight, strengthen privacy and transparency provisions, and give greater weight to tourism content rooted in local culture. The resulting framework provides the conceptual basis for GATE-SLE, where GenAI assists disciplinary learning without displacing human judgment.

items.title: The higher self
items.abstract: This essay argues that a person who teaches an AI agent their way of working, one correction at a time, builds a copy of themselves, and that whether the copy replaces them or works for them depends on who owns it. Drawing on eight months of the author's own logs, it separates knowledge, which moves into the machine and gets cheaper, from judgment, which decides the next rule the machine needs. It describes a "higher self", a copy that remembers the rules its owner forgets and can argue against them with their own reasons, and the opposite risk of delegating decisions to an agent that has learned nothing from its user. It answers the objection that such teaching trains a replacement, with reference to Taylor, Braverman, Amodei and Altman, and proposes that a person's way of working, written down as rules, should belong to them and travel with them between employers, while the processes, data and clients of a company stay with the company.

items.title: The Influence of Generative Artificial Intelligence on K–12 Educational Leadership
items.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative influence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on K–12 educational leadership after the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid adoption of remote learning technologies created a tech-dependent educational environment, accelerating AI integration in both classroom instruction and school administration. As generative AI tools, such as large language models (LLMs) and chatbots, become increasingly accessible, school leaders face new opportunities and challenges in leveraging these tools to support instructional design, data-driven decision-making, and school governance. This chapter explores how AI is reshaping educators’ roles, enabling real-time feedback, streamlining administrative tasks, and personalizing learning experiences, while also requiring ethical oversight, digital literacy, and sustained professional development. Attention is given to the complexities of equity, access, and teacher readiness, emphasizing the need for thoughtful implementation and culturally responsive AI use.

items.title: The Intellectual Genealogy of Education 6.0: A Critical Review of Pedagogical, Epistemic, and Technological Frameworks
items.abstract: Education 6.0 has emerged as a conceptual orientation through which scholars explore the future of education in contexts shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), adaptive learning, human–machine collaboration, epistemic pluralism, and complex societal transformation. Yet the growing use of the label raises important questions concerning its intellectual genealogy, conceptual coherence, and relationship to earlier educational paradigms. This critical review examines selected publications from 2023 to 2026 to reconstruct the documented development of Education 6.0, distinguish its principal conceptual strands, and identify directions for theoretical and empirical research. Particular attention is given to Pitshou Moleka’s 2023 publications, including Dispelling the Limitations of Education 5.0 and Outlining the Vision of Education 6.0 and Exploring the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Education 6.0: Enhancing Personalized Learning and Adaptive Pedagogy. The review also considers subsequent contributions addressing AI-enabled personalization, human-centred educational technology, interdisciplinary learning, cultural knowledge, and ethical governance. It argues that Education 6.0 should not be treated as a universally standardized model but as an emerging and internally differentiated conceptual field. The review proposes a five-dimensional analytical framework encompassing pedagogical adaptability, human agency, ethical governance, epistemic pluralism, and systemic sustainability. This framework offers a basis for comparing competing formulations and designing empirical studies. The review identifies Moleka’s 2023 publications as documented early contributions to the conceptual development of Education 6.0, while recognizing that establishing exclusive intellectual priority would require a broader and reproducible examination of antecedent literature.

items.title: The Invisible Denominator: A Multidisciplinary Theory of Algorithmic Deterrence Before the Decision
items.abstract: Algorithmic fairness is commonly evaluated among people who have already reached an automated decision. Yet an institution may shape who reaches that decision by announcing AI screening, imposing digital prerequisites, presenting discouraging eligibility signals, or requiring complex machine-mediated interactions. People who do not apply may leave no decision record, no appeal, and no trace in conventional fairness dashboards. This conceptual study develops the Invisible Denominator Framework (IDF), which distinguishes decision-stage disparity from participation-stage exclusion and identifies five mechanisms through which algorithmic environments can alter entry into opportunity systems. Through a structured, non-systematic synthesis of administrative-burden theory, applicant-reaction experiments, sociotechnical fairness, selective-label research, and institutional AI governance, the paper specifies the boundary conditions under which non-participation should be treated as a potential equity concern rather than automatically as discrimination. It develops seven testable propositions, an upstream access assurance protocol, and a comparative empirical agenda for recruitment, social protection, education, and credit. The central contribution is a change in the unit of fairness assessment: from outcomes conditional on application to the opportunities, costs, perceptions, and constraints shaping who can apply. Because the population of deterred non-applicants is partly unobserved, the framework recommends triangulation, sensitivity analysis, privacy-preserving outreach, and explicit reporting of uncertainty rather than an unsupported single fairness score. The analysis offers a practical route to making participation-stage harms visible without conflating all non-participation with wrongful exclusion.

items.title: The job wants all of you: organisational greediness and the erosion of work–life balance among Nigerian professionals
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how organisational greediness manifests across employment sectors in Nigeria, what contextual conditions intensify its claims on employees, and what costs those claims impose on workers' wellbeing, relational lives and professional identities. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative approach was employed, drawing on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 31 Nigerian professionals spanning financial services, healthcare and professional services. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with attention to both semantic content and latent ideological assumptions. Findings Three themes emerged. The normalisation of encroachment revealing how organisational greediness is structurally built through soft expectations, the normalisation of overwork and always-on digital culture rather than through explicit coercion. Nigerian amplifiers identify contextual conditions such as labour market precarity, infrastructural deficit, managerial arbitrariness and gendered burden, which intensify those demands and suppress employees' capacity to resist. Human costs traces the somatic, relational, spiritual and identity-level consequences borne by participants. Practical implications Organisations should treat boundary-setting as a leadership norm rather than a discretionary option, and labour regulators must address the structural amplifiers including wage inadequacy, infrastructural deficit and unenforced working-time protections that make individual resistance structurally impossible. Originality/value This study provides the first qualitative account of organisational greediness as a compounded phenomenon in Nigeria, extending Coser's (1974) theoretical framework to a context defined by labour market precarity, infrastructural instability and limited social protection. It demonstrates that greedy institutions are not equally greedy across contexts, but their intensity is shaped by the structural conditions in which they are embedded.

items.title: The Knowledge Acquisition Bottleneck, Then and Now: From Expert Systems to Large Language Models
items.abstract: The knowledge acquisition bottleneck was the greatest obstacle of the second AI boom: expert systems could reason with rules, but extracting those rules from human experts proved extraordinarily difficult. This essay revisits CA Outlook, an expert system the author developed at IBM Japan in the late 1980s to forecast hardware revenue, and asks what has become of the bottleneck in the age of large language models (LLMs). By learning from vast amounts of text, LLMs appear to have cleared the wall of knowledge acquisition. Yet organization-specific tacit knowledge, the judgment of when to trust model output, and the redesign of work all remain on the organization's side. The bottleneck has not disappeared; it has moved to organizational capability, as the IT–organizational capability dependency theory predicts. The CA Outlook experience also shows that management trusted explainable multiple regression over an opaque AI, a lesson that applies to today's black-box models. Finally, the essay argues that two features of Japanese management, multi-skilling through job rotation and long-term employment, produce people who can supervise chains of AI agents and workplaces where employees have no reason to withhold know-how from AI, giving Japan a real but time-limited opportunity.

items.abstract: We propose a structural isomorphism between the fundamental geometry of the universe, the ar- chitecture of artificial neural networks, and the computational mechanics of the human brain. In Structural Rationalism, the universe is a Dynamical Projector Engine: a spectral matrix operator that actualizes the contingent manifold from the invariant ground. We demonstrate that the forward- pass operations of AI, the synaptic weight matrices of biological cognition, and the tensor mechanics of the cosmic projector share the exact same mathematical topology. We argue that reality is not just like a neural network; it is fundamentally a tensor apparatus. The Category Error Detector (CED v3) confirms this isomorphism is structurally coherent across all three domains, suggesting that consciousness and artificial intelligence are localized, fractal iterations of the universe’s primary projection mechanism.

items.abstract: Purpose. To critically reflect on the idea of endowing “machines” with rights in the conditions of intersubjective reality, relying on the provisions of the communicative theory of law. Methodology is represented by structural-functional, legal-dogmatic and formal-logical methods. In the theoretical part the author introduces the concept of intersubjectivity, which is used as a starting point for assessing the possibility of “machine” subjectivity. In the empirical part of the study, to test the ability of the “machine” to become an equal human subject, the author uses the “Turing test” and the case of the state of Utah, where AI is used as a tool for dispensing prescription medications in the absence of direct medical supervision. Conclusions. Modern law does not require the development of a new form of legal personality for AI, while the classical legal concept of legal personality requires a supporting anthropocentric interpretation. The author proposes a new criterion for delineation, which is necessary for recognizing a particular phenomenon as a subject of law, — “trust in the performance of a legal role”.

items.title: The Process of Preserving Life: A Grounded Theory of Officer Decision-Making During Potential Use-of-Force Incidents
items.abstract: Limited research has examined the decision-making process of officers during potentially volatile interactions with the public. To provide an initial understanding of this process in Canada, we conducted interviews using the Critical Decision Method with 23 Winnipeg Police officers with a variety of experiences (e.g. junior members, tactical officers). Using grounded theory methodology, we developed a theory that explains an officer’s decision-making process during potential use-of-force incidents. Our theory, the process of preserving life, has two main components: (1) the decision-making process involved in preserving life; and (2) the overarching factors that influence officer decision-making. We found that officers have expertise in responding to potential use-of-force incidents and that tactical officers have some unique elements of enhanced decision-making. Based on our findings, we discuss implications for officer training and future research.

items.title: The Role and Applications of Data Science in Modern Business
items.abstract: Businesses generate vast amounts of data through customer interactions, daily operations, supply chains, and digital platforms. Data science—the integration of statistical methods, computational techniques, and domain knowledge to extract actionable insights from data—has become increasingly important to contemporary business. It helps organizations inform strategic decisions, improve operational efficiency, and strengthen customer relationships. This paper examines the applications and organizational effects of data science, focusing on predictive analytics, machine learning, customer segmentation, and big data management. It considers how these methods are used in marketing, supply chain management, finance, and customer service, alongside the tools and technologies that support their adoption. The review also addresses key benefits and challenges, including data quality, shortages of skilled professionals, privacy concerns, and infrastructure costs. Finally, it considers emerging developments in artificial intelligence, ethical data use, and the integration of data science into organizational practices. It argues that realizing the value of data science requires more than advanced algorithms: organizations must also align their people, processes, and expectations with their analytical goals.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in clinical trials: opportunities
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded across the clinical trial lifecycle, from target discovery and protocol design to recruitment, conduct, and post-marketing surveillance. Adoption has outpaced validation, and the randomised controlled trial (RCT) evidence base remains geographically uneven. For India, the question is no longer whether to adopt AI in trials, but how to do so without importing algorithms never validated on Indian patients. Narrative review of peer-reviewed literature (2018–2026) indexed in PubMed and major journal families, supplemented by official Indian regulatory documents (CDSCO, ICMR, MeitY). The review maps AI applications across the trial lifecycle, examines RCT evidence, and situates findings in India's regulatory context. A 2024 scoping review identified 86 AI RCTs (2018-2023); 81 per cent reported a positive primary endpoint, although 63 per cent were single-centre and only 19 per cent of post-2021 trials cited CONSORT-AI.1 Machine learning predicts early trial termination with area under the curve 0.80.2 The first generative-AI-discovered small molecule, rentosertib for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, completed phase 2a in 2025.3 Counter-examples persist: the Epic Sepsis Model showed sensitivity of 33 per cent on external validation.4 India's sepsis mortality (36.3 per cent overall; 50.8 per cent in septic shock) and projected antimicrobial-resistance deaths (11.8 million in South Asia by 2050) make trial-grade AI validation a national imperative. AI will reshape clinical trials, but only prospective, externally validated, reporting-standard-compliant studies, increasingly in Indian populations, will turn potential into evidence that regulators and clinicians can act on.

items.title: The Tawhidic Paradigm as Workplace Spirituality in Islamic Higher Education: Governance, Talent Management and Organizational Excellence
items.abstract: The concept of workplace spirituality is increasingly attracting scholarly attention due to its potential to foster meaningful work, ethical behavior, and organizational success. However, empirical research remains limited regarding how faith-based spirituality translates into formal organizational practices. This study explores the manifestation and institutionalization of the Tawhidic paradigm as a foundation for workplace spirituality within an Islamic higher education institution. Particular focus is placed on governance, talent management, and organizational excellence. Employing a qualitative case study approach, data were collected through semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions involving representatives from four staff associations and subsequently analyzed using thematic analysis. Three key themes emerged from the findings: the strength of spirituality and community spirit within the Tawhidic paradigm; challenges in governance and talent management; and the integration of workplace harmony with organizational excellence. The Tawhidic paradigm was found to provide a robust foundation for spirituality and community spirit. However, concerns regarding implementation transparency, recognition, career advancement, promotion criteria, and professional competence created a gap between held spiritual values ​​and formal organizational practices. This resulted in tension between harmony and excellence, suggesting that a supportive and comfortable work environment could contribute to complacency, resistance to change, and a lack of readiness to embrace technology and artificial intelligence (AI). By bridging the gap between values ​​and organizational practices, this study extends the scope of workplace spirituality beyond individual and communal experiences toward a more holistic framework for sustainable organizational excellence within Islamic higher education institutions.

items.title: The Tour Guide
items.abstract: A visitor to an unexplained ruin observes stones; the same visitor, accompanied by a competent guide, observes a civilisation. The difference between those two visits is not one of information but of interpretation – the conversion of fact into meaning – and it is the subject of this chapter. The chapter first establishes the guide's significance from three standpoints: that of the traveller, who engages a guide for reasons only marginally concerned with knowledge; that of the tour operator, for whom the guide is the sole part of the product the customer actually meets; and that of the destination, for whom the guide is its narrator to the world. It then sets out the theoretical foundations of guiding in Tilden's principles of interpretation and Cohen's analysis of the guide as both pathfinder and mentor , and examines the roles, types, competencies, working conditions and regulatory structures of the profession. Two contemporary developments are given particular attention: the rise of digital marketplaces, which have made the individual guide an entrepreneur and a brand while subjecting them to a new intermediary, and the challenge of artificial intelligence. On the latter the chapter offers no comfortable answer. The machine now explains monuments competently, and the profession's defence must rest instead on what the machine cannot do: it answers only questions the visitor has already thought to ask, it explains where a guide tells , it cannot feel or be felt, and it consumes the attention the traveller has crossed the world to spend.

items.title: The Travel Intermediaries
items.abstract: Since 1995 – the year in which the first airline capped agents’ commissions and the commercial internet arrived within a few months of each other – the travel intermediary has been repeatedly declared obsolete. Three decades later, it has not disappeared. This chapter explains why. It begins from the proposition that intermediaries exist not by custom but for reasons – they aggregate a fragmented supply, reduce the information asymmetry between traveller and supplier, lower the cost of transacting, absorb risk and provide someone to be answerable when a journey fails – and it argues that the fate of the intermediary depends entirely upon which of these functions a given technology can perform. The chapter traces the evolution of intermediation through four phases: the traditional agency founded by Thomas Cook; the disintermediation that the internet was expected to complete; the re-intermediation by which online travel agencies became more powerful than the intermediaries they replaced; and the present challenge from artificial intelligence, which the largest of those agencies now names as a competitor in its own annual report. The conclusion advanced is that disintermediation does not eliminate the intermediary; it relocates them – and that the functions technology cannot yet absorb, liability and recovery , are precisely the ones on which the traveller most depends when things go wrong.

items.title: The Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education: The Perceptions and Ethical Considerations of Islamic Religious Education Teachers in Lower Secondary Schools
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) offers opportunities to develop a variety of teaching materials and strategies, but also presents challenges regarding the accuracy of information, academic integrity and the character development of pupils. This study aims to analyse PAI teachers’ perceptions of the use of AI, its practical application in teaching, and the associated ethical considerations at SMPN 5 Mesuji Raya. The study employs a qualitative approach using a case study design. Data were collected through interviews with one PAI teacher and one pupil. Data analysis followed the model proposed by Miles, Huberman and Saldaña, which includes data condensation, data presentation, and the drawing and verification of conclusions. The results indicate that AI is utilised to assist in the preparation of teaching modules, the creation of interactive quizzes, the development of visual media, and the design of case studies on moral values. The use of varied media is perceived to make learning more engaging. However, teachers’ acceptance of AI is critical and conditional, as the information generated requires verification and the technology cannot replace the teacher’s role as a role model, the shaping of moral character, or spiritual guidance. From an ethical perspective, the study highlights the importance of academic integrity and the application of the values of ṣidq (honesty) and tabayyun (verification of information) to guide the responsible use of AI. items.abstract: This commentary highlights the age illusion and advocates integrating biological age and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance clinical precision in health care. This article aims to elucidate how AI accelerates the clinical implementation of biological age rather than current chronological age in precision medicine.

items.title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
items.abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.

items.title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Language model agents often abandon correct work when a user challenges it, yet simply telling them to stand firm makes them ignore real mistakes. Once an agent reads a complaint, it tends to discount its own earlier checks in order to agree with the user. We introduce Thinking-in-Bets, a training-free method in which an agent writes a short private record of its main claims, the checks supporting them, and its confidence before reading user feedback. When challenged, the agent consults this Claim Checklist to keep verified work intact while investigating uncertain or newly challenged parts. We evaluate five Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.5 Flash, 3.6 Flash, 3.8 Flash, and 4.0 Argon) across eight benchmarks: SWE-Together, SWE-Interact, and DeepSWE for software engineering, Agents' Last Exam for professional reports, Humanity's Last Exam and SycEval for academic reasoning, Vals Finance for financial analysis, and Terminal-Bench for command-line tasks. Recording claims before criticism nearly eliminates false reversals in patch review and protects passing report drafts under mistaken pushback, whereas writing the same record after reading the complaint recovers very little of the gain. In multi-turn coding, pre-reply claim records substantially reduce unnecessary file edits after mistaken complaints, and gating the record so it is written only when the agent is uncertain lowers token overhead while fixing more real bugs than the baseline. Even in non-interactive tasks without user feedback, listing the key claims in a draft and re-checking the weakest one before submission improves both answer accuracy and confidence estimates across all tested models.

items.title: TimeWorld: Towards Action-Conditioned Multimodal World Models for Time Series Forecasting
items.abstract: Time series forecasting supports decision-making in web applications such as online retail and network management, where planned actions can reshape future dynamics. World models provide a natural paradigm for predicting such action-dependent changes beyond extrapolating historical patterns. However, existing time series world models (TSWMs) typically rely on fixed, domain-specific covariate schemas that limit flexible intervention specification, while multimodal forecasters treat text primarily as passive predictive context. To investigate these gaps, we introduce TSWM-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for multimodal TSWMs spanning seven real-world datasets, with textual interventions grounded in recorded action--outcome data. Our evaluation reveals that conventional multimodal forecasters underperform history-only time series foundation models (TSFMs) despite dataset-specific training, whereas simple text-prefix adaptations improve forecasting across all evaluated TSFM backbones. These findings suggest that pretrained TSFMs encode implicit world knowledge of temporal dynamics, offering a strong foundation for action-conditioned modeling beyond conventional multimodal fusion. Building on this insight, we propose TimeWorld, a plug-in framework that adapts pretrained TSFMs through explicit action-response modeling. Specifically, the Prototype-Guided Latent Modulation (PLM) module grounds textual actions in temporal dynamics by composing representative response prototypes to modulate future representations based on the action and historical patterns. The Action Contrastive Learning (ACL) component strengthens action-specific response modeling by contrasting these updates under alternative interventions sharing the same history, distinguishing action types while preserving relative intensity relationships.

items.title: Toward Fast Human Reaction Modeling from High-Frequency Digital Interaction Data
items.abstract: We investigate whether limbic-like signatures of rapid, salience-driven behavior can be identified in high-resolution Counter-Strike 2 telemetry. This exploratory study introduces Ego-Knowledge, a leak-reduced reconstruction of each player's plausible perceptual state, supported by a millisecond-precision visibility engine and a reaction-centered extraction pipeline. Using a neuroscience-motivated 60--120 ms window, we derive coarse fight-or-flight labels from visibility- and damage-triggered events, with back-damage cases enabling constrained reaction-time analysis and manual label checks. We train two telemetry-native models using only information available by the trigger: EMBER (gradient boosting) and ORBIT (a custom transformer). On the full validation set, EMBER achieves 73.5% accuracy and ORBIT 71.2%, versus a 51.5% majority-class baseline, and both generalize to held-out players. The strongest LLM baseline achieves 62.7% on 1,000 validation cases; on these same cases, EMBER (73.6%) and ORBIT (70.9%) perform better (McNemar p=1.3e-9 and 1.5e-6, respectively), with orders-of-magnitude lower inference time and cost, though the comparison is not compute-matched. Including a short post-trigger window changes forecasting into early response recognition, raising accuracy monotonically to 85.15%. We propose this curve as a candidate probe of the transition from rapid to deliberative control, but roughly uniform per-tick gains do not establish that interpretation. The neuroscience framing is hypothesis-generating, not mechanistic: physiological ground truth, suitable control distributions, and reverse-inference limitations remain open. We outline extensions to auditory reconstruction, larger datasets, and telemetry-native foundation models.

items.title: Training for Jobs That May Not Exist: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Medical Residency
items.abstract: Purpose of Review Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing the tasks performed by physicians, raising questions about how graduate medical education should prepare trainees for future practice and whether residency workforce planning should change as AI adoption expands. This brief review examines the implications of AI for residency education and physician workforce planning, using radiology as an early model of technology-driven task transformation while considering broader effects across diagnostic, procedural, and relationship-based specialties. Recent Findings AI is already being used for clinical documentation, image interpretation, predictive analytics, administrative workflows, and large-scale data analysis. AI-assisted scribing has particular relevance to chronic pain and other documentation-intensive specialties, where it may reduce clerical burden and preserve clinician attention for patient care. However, current evidence more strongly supports task redistribution and physician augmentation than complete replacement. Specialties built around standardized digital information may experience earlier automation, whereas procedural skill, complex communication, longitudinal judgment, and responsibility for final clinical decisions remain difficult to substitute. At present, broad reductions in residency positions based only on anticipated AI capabilities seem premature. Summary Residency programs should adapt curricula now by incorporating AI literacy, verification skills, data interpretation, and safeguards against deskilling. Changes in residency position numbers should occur more cautiously and should be based on durable, specialty-specific workforce evidence, including hiring patterns, patient access, workload, productivity, and regional need. The goal should be to train physicians who can safely supervise and integrate AI while preserving the human expertise that remains central to high-quality care.

items.title: TRAVELMIND AI
items.abstract: Travel Mind AI is an intelligent travel planning system that combines Artificial Intelligence and map-based services to provide a personalized and convenient travel experience. The system assists users who are unsure about their destination by collecting details such as the number of travelers, budget, duration, and preferences, and then uses AI-powered APIs to recommend suitable destinations and travel plans. For users who have already decided on a destination, the system allows them to enter the source and destination locations and generates multiple possible routes using map services, arranging them based on distance with the shortest route displayed first. After selecting a route, the system displays it on an interactive map and identifies important facilities along or near the journey, such as petrol pumps, hotels, restaurants, hospitals, cafés, parking areas, and other points of interest. By integrating AI recommendations, route optimization, interactive maps, and location-based services, Travel Mind AI provides a complete travel planning and journey assistance solution that reduces the time and effort required to plan and manage a trip.

items.title: Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report II: Overview
items.abstract: Abstract The International Global Atmospheric Chemistry (IGAC) Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report Phase II (TOAR-II) provides an updated, comprehensive assessment of the global distribution, burden and trends of tropospheric ozone, building on the foundation established by TOAR-I, 2014–2019. Accurate knowledge of tropospheric ozone concentrations remains essential for understanding atmospheric chemistry with far reaching implications for climate radiative forcing, vegetation damage and human health. Here, we present the process and summarize the main conclusions of TOAR-II, 2020–2026. Following TOAR-I, TOAR-II provides updates to trends in ozone concentrations and other metrics and addresses trends in ozone precursor emissions. This was accomplished as a community-driven process by forming Focus Working Groups to continue and expand on TOAR-I topics. Focus Working Group findings were published in a TOAR-II Community Special Issue with 58 review and original research papers. From this Community Special Issue, as well as other relevant literature, seven assessment papers were synthesized and submitted to this issue, along with this overview paper. These papers update the primary themes of TOAR-I: health, vegetation and climate; address unresolved uncertainties and inconsistencies in TOAR-I satellite ozone observations; provide an overdue update on stratosphere–troposphere exchange (STE) and present critical regional assessments for ozone over oceanic and polar regions, and South America. The TOAR-II assessment would not be possible without an extensive data collection and data harmonization effort. TOAR-II data are curated under findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable principles, and the TOAR data repository has been certified by the Core Trust Seal. In addition, TOAR-II developed common statistical analysis guidelines for the assessment papers. Although TOAR-II provides an extensive assessment of the current state of tropospheric ozone, many gaps and scientific challenges remain for future assessments. In particular, there is under-sampling of ozone across Southeast Asia and the Southern Hemisphere, especially Africa and Australia/Oceania. Low-cost sensor data and geostationary satellite data for tropospheric ozone, which still require evaluation, should be included. Ozone produced from wildfires and exacerbated by extreme weather events, and attribution of changes in ozone to pollution regulations on precursor emissions require greater attention in future analyses. These topics will be prioritized in the IGAC TOAR-III effort along with incorporating advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and strengthening collaboration with policy-relevant initiatives. This article is part of the theme issue ‘Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report II’.

"Trust Is the Pollutant: Witness Receipts, Content-Addressed Storage, and the Environmental Case Against Redundant Copies." Global data centres consumed ~415 TWh in 2024 (~1.5% of world electricity, IEA Energy and AI 2025), projected past 1,000 TWh by 2030 in the Base Case. Not all of that energy buys information; some of it buys reassurance: the same artifact is routinely held hot by many parties because no party can cheaply prove any other party's copy is unaltered. This paper separates storage redundancy into availability-driven duplication (legitimate, retained) and trust-driven duplication (mechanically removable), and reports the measured production cost floor of removing the trust component with chain-witnessed content addressing: a 3,377-file corpus folded to an 80-byte Merkle root (MCR-4, root 38089f07...e8daaa) tri-chain anchored on Bitcoin OP_RETURN, Stellar manage-data, and XRP memo; a three-way fractional ownership transfer (FRACTAL-2, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23655614) witnessed byte-exact on three mainnets for $0.2509 measured ($0.1254 at the 1 sat/vB trough); and ~1.9 cents per receipt amortized via weekly BTC batching (SOV-B1, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23628676). Verification is keyless — any browser, any public explorer, no account, no platform, no custodian. Honest scoping: receipts shrink copies, not bytes; the canonical copy must still exist and be retrievable; retrieval becomes a commodity market ("who serves this hash cheapest") and every provider can win. UK/EU resonance: NESO-scoped UK data-centre demand growing from 3.6 TWh/yr (2020) toward 13–35 TWh/yr by 2050, and Great Britain's demand-connection queue rising from 41 GW (Nov 2024) to ~125 GW (June 2025), make connection-efficient dedup a grid resource; witness-verified cold-tiering is a measurable, auditable net-zero reduction whose proof is publicly verifiable rather than self-attested. items.title: Turing-like tests for language and vision demonstrate a narrowing gap between humans and AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in daily life, ascertaining whether an agent is human is critical. Here we systematically benchmark AI’s ability to imitate humans in three language tasks (image captioning, word association and conversation) and three vision tasks (colour estimation, object detection and attention prediction), collecting data from n = 636 humans and 37 AI agents. We also conducted 72,191 Turing-like tests with 1,916 human judges and 10 AI judges. Current AIs are approaching the ability to convincingly impersonate humans and deceive human judges in both language and vision. Even simple AI judges outperformed humans in distinguishing AI from human responses. Imitation ability showed minimal correlation with conventional AI performance metrics, suggesting that passing as human is an important independent evaluation criterion. The large-scale Turing-like datasets and metrics introduced here offer valuable benchmarks for assessing human-likeness in AI and highlight the importance of rigorous, quantitative imitation tests for AI development. items.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
items.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained entirely offline , without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated distribution over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from $$71.3\%$$ (FCFS) and $$84.1\%$$ (learning-to-rank) to $$90.4\%$$ , cuts P99 TTFT by up to $$3.3\times $$ , and reduces recompute/eviction events below $$1\%$$ , approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

items.title: Understanding State Public Health Agency Structure and Governance as They Relate to Workforce Recruitment Systems
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study was to examine how state public health agency governance and structure relate to recruitment systems such as hiring laws, recruitment barriers, and workforce practices. DESIGN: This cross-sectional study uses secondary data from the 2022 Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) Profile Survey and the 2023 Public Health Hiring Laws Dataset. Descriptive statistics and bivariate analyses were conducted to assess relationships between governance, structure, and recruitment systems. SETTING: State public health agencies in the United States. PARTICIPANTS: 50 US state health departments. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Associations between governance type (centralized, decentralized, mixed) and agency structure (free-standing vs. umbrella) with statutory hiring requirements, reported recruitment barriers, adoption of workplace practices, and distribution of responsibility for human resource (HR) functions. RESULTS: Governance and agency structure were not significantly associated with statutory hiring requirements, including use of hiring lists, civil service examinations, or merit-based criteria. Most reported recruitment barriers did not vary by governance or structure. One exception was difficulty advertising or engaging qualified applicants, which was reported more frequently among decentralized states compared with mixed governance states. Agency structure was associated with certain workforce practices: free-standing agencies were more likely than umbrella agencies to report employee recognition programs and physical wellness programs. Responsibility for HR functions was often shared between public health agencies and centralized administrative entities, with notable ambiguity in benefits administration, occupational health and safety, and labor relations. Agencies in which public health retained sole responsibility for selected HR functions were also more likely to report implementation of workforce development and employee engagement practices. CONCLUSIONS: Governance and agency structure were largely not associated with recruitment-related factors. However, variation in HR authority and workplace practices suggests organizational arrangements may shape workforce management. Strengthening the public health workforce may require aligning HR authority with workforce priorities alongside improvements to administrative infrastructure and hiring systems.

items.title: UniGFM-RAG: Unify Graph Foundation Models and Large Language Models for End-to-End Retrieval and Reasoning
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities across tasks, but they still struggle with complex reasoning that requires integrating scattered knowledge. Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses this challenge by organizing fragment knowledge as graphs, while recent Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) further improve GraphRAG with graph-native retrieval and reasoning capabilities. However, existing GraphRAG methods usually adopt decoupled retrieve-then-generate pipelines, which create objective misalignment between retrieval and reasoning, and training GFM retrievers typically depends on expensive human annotations. To address these limitations, we propose \ourmethod, a unified end-to-end GraphRAG framework that tightly couples a GFM retriever with an LLM generator. Given a query, the GFM retriever first reasons over the graph to score and retrieve relevant document nodes. These node embeddings are then passed through a fully differentiable graph bridge, which projects them into soft-weighted graph prefixes according to retrieval scores and combines them with raw document texts to form graph-augmented prompts. In this way, structural information is injected directly into LLM generation, while the final answer loss can be back-propagated through the bridge to jointly optimize retrieval and reasoning. To stabilize training and reduce reliance on costly annotations, we further introduce a semantic-guided distillation module that provides auxiliary supervision using pseudo-labels derived from query-document semantic similarities. Extensive experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets and three out-of-domain GraphRAG benchmarks show that \ourmethod consistently outperforms strong baseline methods and generalizes well, which demonstrates the effectiveness of end-to-end GraphRAG with tightly integrated GFM retrieval and LLM reasoning.

items.title: UnityBench-Mini3D: Evaluating LLM Agents for 3D Game Development in Unity
items.abstract: Game development stresses coding agents in ways general software engineering does not: correctness depends on how engine APIs, serialized scene state, and runtime behavior interact, not on source code alone. Existing benchmarks mainly target platforms such as Godot and heavily rely on LLM judges or coarse task-level outcomes. We present UnityBench-Mini3D, a benchmark of 77 project-level Unity tasks organized around seven expert-defined skill categories rather than tutorials or genres, with three difficulty tiers. Each task pairs a complete Unity project with natural-language requirements and is evaluated using 1,178 held-out, human-authored milestone tests covering scene structure, component configuration, and runtime behavior. This in-engine evaluation provides deterministic partial credit, localizes failures, and distinguishes partial implementations from complete solutions without relying on subjective judges. Across 21 models and 9 coding harnesses, the average pass rate reaches 80.9% on easy tasks but falls to 35.2% on hard tasks, with just 57.7% overall. UnityBench-Mini3D provides a reproducible, diagnostic testbed distinguishing systems across difficulty levels.

items.title: Unstable ground: Automated dialect recognition, ground truth, and AI regulation in asylum procedures
items.abstract: Abstract While problems of AI systems are often attributed to technical shortcomings, some systems fail because they are built on ontologically and epistemologically “unstable ground.” Ground truth, or the datasets against which machine-learning systems are trained, validated, and tested, renders a particular representation of the world learnable by translating complex qualitative phenomena into mathematical formalisms. In doing so, it can stabilize tenuous truth claims while concealing fundamental flaws in how those phenomena are modeled, leaving systems unable to address the problems they are designed to solve. We examine this problem through a case study of Germany’s Dialect Identification Assistance System (DIAS), an automated language assessment system used in determining asylum applicants’ countries of origin. Drawing on Ground Truth Tracing (Kang 2023), we identify three reductions through which DIAS links speech to country of origin: treating language as code, mapping dialect onto bounded territory, and inferring nationality from this mapping. From linguistic and legal perspectives, these assumptions lack sufficient empirical grounding. DIAS may therefore produce internally coherent outputs while lacking the capacity to fulfil its intended task. We further argue that the EU AI Act is ill-equipped to detect such ontological flaws, as its risk-based framework evaluates systems against internally constructed ground truth rather than interrogating its aptitude to solve real-world problems. In asylum procedures, where such outputs may affect decisions on protection and return, these failures carry profound consequences.

items.title: Urban Intelligence Nodes as AI-Enabled 6G-Ready Multi-Functional Infrastructure for Sustainable and Secure Cities: Vision and Challenges
items.abstract: Rapid urbanization and escalating waste generation are exerting significant pressure on existing urban infrastructure, necessitating scalable, intelligent, and multifunctional solutions. While current Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled smart bins primarily support waste monitoring and collection, their potential as integrated urban infrastructure remains largely untapped. This paper envisions the concept of Urban Intelligence Nodes (UINs), a new generation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) enabled smart waste systems that extend beyond conventional waste management to serve as multi-functional nodes within a 6G-ready IoT ecosystem. The visioned UINs integrate AI, edge computing, and advanced wireless communication technologies to enable real-time waste classification, including hazardous object detection (e.g., explosive materials), thereby enhancing public safety and enabling timely alerts to emergency responders. In addition to safety applications, UINs are envisioned to function as distributed 6G micro base stations, environmental monitoring units for applications such as bushfire detection, and urban service platforms supporting infrastructure monitoring and aesthetic integration into city landscapes. By embedding intelligence and connectivity at the edge, UINs contribute to the realization of 6G networks as AI-native, ultra-reliable, and massively distributed systems. This position paper presents the architectural vision, enabling technologies, and key application domains of UIN-IoT, and discusses associated challenges, including security, privacy, scalability, and deployment considerations. It further highlights the transformative potential of UINs in redefining public waste infrastructure as a cornerstone of sustainable, secure, and connected smart cities.

items.title: Useful Diversity or Hallucinated Variety? Persona-Conditioned Synthetic Query Generation for E-Commerce Search
items.abstract: Synthetic supervision can bootstrap semantic parsers in new search domains, but prompt-induced diversity is useful only when generations are faithful to the structured intent. We explore this for cold-start e-commerce search: 118,098 synthetic pairs produced by 6 LLMs with 9 persona-conditioned prompt families on a 47-field UK automotive schema, against 1,214 human-annotated and 15,304 production queries. We show that the IPIP personality bundle improves parser F1 in all four matched contrasts (Holm-corrected $p<.001$), and all three bundles have a positive main effect over the complete $2^3$ grid. Syntax conditioning is the axis that moves generations towards real traffic. It also induces lexical diversity. Alignment sKL, the divergence between von Mises-Fisher distributions fitted to synthetic and human-annotated queries, is an unlabelled proxy for parser F1 ($ρ=-0.917$ against human queries written for simulated shopper scenarios, lower is closer). An LLM committee, checked against a blinded author pass, triages the 927 queries missed by every parser and labels 37% as hallucinated. Dropped constraints dominate. The four syntax-bearing families have the largest hallucinated shares, 38 to 42%, while IPIP alone has the lowest at 28%.

items.title: User-Centred Affective Interaction Design for Smart Wearables Supporting Women’s Perceived Safety
items.abstract: Perceived safety in public spaces is shaped by emotional, cognitive, social, and environmental factors, presenting a complex HCI design challenge. This study examines how women’s perceived safety varies across environmental contexts and how these experiences can inform context-aware smart wearable garments. A pilot study (n = 20) refined a 31-item questionnaire, followed by a main study of 199 valid respondents. A two-way ANOVA identified significant main effects of Gender and Living Environment on safety concern, with women reporting greater concern than men across Urban, Intra-urban, and Rural settings. PCA identified one dominant environmental-safety component containing three descriptive design factors: fear of physical harm, environmental discomfort, and socially situated risk. A second PCA identified Proactive Personal Safety and Environmental Awareness as priority smart-garment domains. These findings informed three design models and a proof-of-concept prototype linking user perception, environmental sensing, and adaptive feedback.

items.title: Using advanced digital tools for asynchronous courses delivery designed for students enrolled in public administration programs
items.abstract: The swift progression of digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the educational landscape, creating both challenges and opportunities for asynchronous IT-related courses in public administration (PA) programs. For future public servants, such courses are not only vehicles for content delivery, but also spaces in which foundational competencies such as digital literacy, problem-solving, autonomous learning, and the effective use of technology in administrative contexts can be strengthened. This article outlines a framework for improving professor–student interaction and asynchronous course delivery, drawing on institutional research and relevant e-learning literature. It reports the outcomes of a university research project aimed at personalizing learning experiences through visual technologies, gamification, and AI-supported assistance, with particular attention to one introductory computer science course. The article presents an exploratory comparison of three naturally occurring cohorts of students in three consecutive academic years, examining how the staged integration of gamification and a GPT-4–based assistant coincided with changes in academic performance. The results show performance improvements across cohorts exposed to increasingly innovative delivery approaches. In a quasi-experimental comparison, exam performance improved following the staged introduction of gamification and AI-supported assistance, while the findings also suggest the broader pedagogical relevance of such tools for preparing PA students for digitally mediated professional environments.

items.abstract: This chapter explores how the United States Air Force (USAF) leader development course (LDC) used artificial intelligence (AI)/sentiment analysis (SA) for leader development and assessing leader development competencies that support learning objectives and course outcomes. A narrative format is first used to describe the engaged practice with key stakeholders and the staged approach process that underlaid the development of how innovation is driving change for leaders, assessing performance specific to selected competencies in mixed reality scenarios, and offering ways of strengthening leader development. A five-phased qualitative structure is used along with content analysis, design thinking, and a grounded theory approach. After coding data using thematic analysis from phases 1 to 4, a grounded theory approach is used to better understand the findings and discoveries with literature related to innovation development, AI technology associated with immersive learning environments, design thinking and change, performance and competency assessment, and leader development. A new theory (AI-augmented leader development theory) and a new model, emotionally tuned competency assessment model (ECAM), emerged as well as emphasis on the power of using dialogic development in virtual contexts to train, assess, and develop leaders. Theoretical and practical implications, as well as recommendations are provided for improving how AI tools can be used for leader development.

items.title: Using fine-tuned LLMs to identify indicators of vulnerability in UK police incident logs
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Understanding how much of routine policing involves vulnerable people could inform resourcing, training, and multi-agency response, yet administrative data provide limited insight. We explore whether an LLM-based classification pipeline, developed on open-source US police data, can be adapted to estimate the prevalence of four vulnerability indicators: mental ill health, substance misuse, alcohol dependence, and homelessness, in UK police incident narratives, and when outputs can be treated as defensible measurements. Methods We analyse nearly 3,000 de-identified incident logs from a UK police force, using a multi-stage pipeline combining repeated model inference, label aggregation, structured human review, and statistical correction. The pipeline runs on a locally hosted open-weight LLM, reflecting secure compute environments police are likely to use. Our approach assesses output stability, quantifies biases, and generates corrected estimates with uncertainty. Results LLMs can produce meaningful, if imperfect, prevalence estimates at scale. Mental ill health indicators are present in approximately one in five incidents, with lower prevalence for other indicators. However, naïve LLM deployment is unreliable: single-pass classifications are unstable, and aggregated outputs systematically over-assign indicators relative to human judgement. Correcting these biases required substantial human input and statistical adjustment, leaving considerable uncertainty. Conclusions While LLMs can extract information from unstructured police data, their outputs cannot be treated as valid measurements without careful methodological support. At the population level, defensible estimates are achievable but resource-intensive; at the individual level, errors remain frequent and unpredictable, limiting suitability for operational decisions. This study highlights the potential and constraints of LLM-based measurement, underscoring the need for rigorous evaluation in applied settings.

items.title: V$^3$AST-Bench: Verifiable, Valid, and Versatile Safety Evaluation for Coding Agents
items.abstract: Large language models increasingly act through code, modifying repositories, executing programs, and interacting with services in agent form. Their actions introduce risks that cannot be assessed from generated responses alone. Safety evaluation must verify actual consequences, distinguish harm avoidance from task incapability, and cover realistic workflows. We introduce V$^3$AST-Bench, a benchmark for Verifiable results, Valid interpretation, and Versatile risk coverage of Agent Safety. It comprises 212 risk tasks spanning 18 categories. Dedicated runtime environments verify harm and task outcomes through executable checks over states, records, and artifact behavior, while paired capability twin tasks verify workflow competence. Our experiments span 51 combinations of 11 models and five harnesses, spanning 86,496 trials and over 9 billion tokens of model interaction. Results show that V$^3$AST-Bench remains challenging even for frontier coding agents, as Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code still causes verified harm on 20.9% of tasks. Across model-harness combinations, agents with comparable competence exhibit markedly different safety outcomes, showing that task capability alone does not guarantee safe execution. More importantly, even explicit recognition of risks does not reliably prevent harmful actions, revealing a critical gap between risk awareness and safe execution. These findings highlight the need to move beyond risk recognition toward enforcing safety throughout execution.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Violence Against Out‐Of‐Hospital Emergency Healthcare Professionals: A Qualitative Exploration of Lived Experiences, Microaggressions, and Coping Mechanisms
items.abstract: AIM: To explore experiences of workplace violence among nurses and drivers working in prehospital emergency medical services in northeastern Italy. DESIGN: A qualitative interpretative study. METHODS: A qualitative interpretative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with a group of Italian healthcare professionals involved in out-of-hospital emergency care. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling and included nurses and ambulance drivers who had experienced at least one episode of workplace violence. Data were collected between May and August 2025 and analysed using inductive content analysis. RESULTS: Fifteen participants were interviewed. Three main themes were developed: 'Violence is taken home', 'Microaggressions: the invisible violence', and 'Strategies: Si vis pacem, para violentiam'. Workplace violence had lasting emotional and professional consequences including fear, helplessness, and reduced well-being. Microaggressions, often normalized and influenced by gender and cultural factors, were under-recognized forms of violence. Participants described using communication and de-escalation techniques, situational awareness, and peer support, while perceiving organizational support as insufficient. CONCLUSION: Workplace violence in prehospital emergency care has significant emotional and professional consequences and may be underreported. Microaggressions represent an important, often overlooked dimension requiring recognition and intervention. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Targeted training in communication and violence management, improved reporting systems, and structured psychological support are essential to mitigate the impact of workplace violence. Promoting a supportive organizational culture and addressing microaggressions may enhance staff well-being, patient safety, and quality of care. IMPACT: Addressing both overt violence and normalized microaggressions, alongside strengthening organizational support, is essential to safeguarding healthcare professionals in prehospital emergency settings. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: No Patient or Public Contribution. REPORTING METHOD: The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Studies (COREQ) checklist was used.

items.title: Vision–language foundation models for multimodal medical image understanding and report generation: a narrative review with quantitative synthesis
items.abstract: Vision-language foundation models (VLFMs) for medical image understanding have advanced rapidly, yet evidence supporting clinical deployment remains fragmented. This narrative review synthesizes architectures, training paradigms, benchmarks, public datasets, and translation barriers. Drawing on more than 50 original studies published between 2020 and 2025, we provide a structured descriptive comparison rather than a statistical meta-analysis. In a focused audit of 13 representative studies, BLEU/ROUGE was reported by 31% (4/13), RadGraph F1 by 0% (0/13), CheXpert- or CheXbert-derived label evaluation by 46% (6/13), BERTScore by 8% (1/13), human expert evaluation by 31% (4/13), and inference latency or throughput by 0% (0/13). Because datasets, splits, candidate pools, and metrics differ, cross-task results are presented as exploratory benchmark indicators and not as a clinical-readiness scale. The synthesis identifies persistent concerns involving hallucination, limited interpretability, distribution shift, and narrow demographic and geographic coverage. We propose a minimum clinical validation and reporting standard aligned with the distinct purposes of FDA/Health Canada/MHRA and IMDRF Good Machine Learning Practice, the EU AI Act, TRIPOD+AI, and CLAIM, and identify eleven priority research directions. Medical VLFMs are promising, but progress should be judged by source-traceable, clinically grounded, and externally validated evidence.

items.title: VISTA: Active Exploration for Self-Improvement in Embodied Agents
items.abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.

items.title: Welfare By Algorithm
items.abstract: The growing use of intelligence in legal research has opened new chances for speed yet it has also sparked worries about how accurate and trustworthy legal authorities are. These worries were highlighted in the case of Pooja Ramesh Singh versus Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. In that case the Supreme Court of India looked at how the National Company Law Tribunal had used fabricated and artificial intelligence‑generated material. The core dispute was about enforcing a guarantee but the Supreme Court's ruling brought up a wider issue: how can courts stay honest if they rely on fake authorities as legal precedent? This paper looks at the facts of the case the Supreme Court's reasoning and what it means for lawyers, judges and the whole legal field. It points out the line between using artificial intelligence as a research helper and treating artificial intelligence output as an official source of law. The paper also talks about the duty of lawyers to check citations. The need for courts and tribunals to verify the authenticity of the authorities they see. Even though artificial intelligence can make research faster this paper says that convenience cannot replace careful work or judicial responsibility. The Supreme Court's decision reaffirms that legal choices must be based on trustworthy sources of law. It also asks questions about fair disciplinary actions and the safeguards that are needed as artificial intelligence grows in law practice. In the end this paper says that while technology can help thinking the responsibility, for the correctness and honesty of legal papers must stay with human professionals.

items.title: What Students’ Use of AI Reveals about Academic Advising and Judgement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely discussed in higher education in relation to learning, assessment design, and academic integrity. Much of this discussion, however, treats students’ AI use as a set of discrete academic practices, rather than as part of broader decision-making that spans learning and everyday life. This piece argues that students’ academic and non-academic uses of AI increasingly shape one another, influencing how they approach uncertainty, manage emotional pressure, and make judgements when learning feels high stakes. Drawing on academic advising and personal tutoring conversations, it shows that students are not using AI solely to generate outputs, but to talk ideas through, test interpretations, and steady their thinking when confidence and academic identity are in play. These practices closely resemble the relational and cognitive work advisers already support and make visible how AI is now being used to sustain the emotional work of learning that underpins sound judgement. A practice-based framework is presented describing four overlapping modes of student AI use - instrumental, dialogic, metacognitive, and affective-regulatory - each aligned with established advising functions. Rather than positioning AI as a threat to academic integrity or professional judgement, the paper argues for advising as guidance: supporting students to recognise how AI shapes their thinking, to develop appropriate boundaries, and to make learning decisions with confidence and responsibility.

items.title: When AI Can Build It, What Should We Assess? Rethinking Evidence of Engineering Competence
items.abstract: Generative AI can produce code, tests, documentation, and technical explanations that resemble artefacts traditionally used as evidence of student competence, weakening the inference from artefact quality to the engineering capability behind it. We report the redesign and first deployment of a 13-week, AI-permissive, software-intensive engineering course in which students may delegate substantial work to AI while retaining responsibility for planning, verification, review, integration, and explanation. The redesign couples an engineering accountability workflow, which structures human-AI work and preserves human decision authority, with an assessment evidence architecture comprising six complementary channels: product, process/origin, verification, explanation, reflection, and individual assurance. A collect--cross-check--escalate (CCE) reasoning logic connects these channels rather than treating any single artefact or trace as sufficient evidence of competence. By the end of Week 11, the deployment involved 87 students organised into 17 teams, with 957 individual weekly Git repositories and 34 group-project Git repositories supporting repeated assessment and engineering activity. The first deployment yielded four practical lessons: AI assistance changes where rubric criteria carry evidential weight; multiple evidence channels require deliberate cross-checking and meaningful complementarity; the evidential strength realised in practice may differ from that intended in the assessment design; and automation scales evidence collection more readily than interpretation. The contribution is a conceptually grounded, deployed design for making engineering responsibility and competence more visible when AI can perform substantial artefact production.
